newsitem.title: USA: Columbia slips on fears of bigger targets.
newsitem.headline: Columbia slips on fears of bigger targets.

text.p: Shares of Columbia/HCA Healthcare Corp on Thursday slipped Thursday amid growing Wall Street concern the federal probe of its Medicare billings could implicate higher-ups in the organization.

Analysts said unrelenting media attention to the Columbia story was keeping investor nerves on edge, with the liklihood that prices would remain depressed for many months to come as the fraud drama plays out in federal courts.
Shares fell 1-1/2 to 31-1/4, their lowest point since FBI agents seized Columbia documents in six states July 16.

Traders focused Thursday on reports that Florida federal prosecutor Kathleen Haley had predicted more indictments would follow those of three mid-level executives already indicted for alleged fraudulent Medicare billings.
Haley also alleged in a Wednesday court hearing in Tampa, Fla., that Columbia had attempted to destroy documents relating to the ongoing probe.
"This wasn't the second shoe to drop. Its about the seventh shoe," said Robert Gold, a health care analyst for S&P Equity Group, who added the media glare was unnerving investors.

"People feel the investigation is going to move up the food chain" to higher executives, he said. "Now there is the question of whether there was an orchestrated scheme in terms of Medicare billings by the corporation itself."
When the FBI searches took place last month, Gold said many investors assumed the probe involved "maybe a few rogue executives trying to boost their hospital's performance" by over-billing Medicare.
"Now there's concern it was a little more intricate -- maybe more centralized. Obviously, it's negative in terms of the perception of the company and the stock," he added.
Nancy Weaver, a Stephens Inc health care analyst, said Columbia's stock -- which peaked at 44-7/8 on February 18 -- would remain in the basement until the federal case unwinds.
"If it takes two years, the stock will be flat for two years. If it's six months, it will respond at that point," she said.

The Nashville-based company announced a sweeping reorganization August 7 meant to blunt the probe and show Columbia's intention to remove temptations for fraud -- most notably its plan to sell or spin off its home health division.
"But the company can't do anything to really restructure the company until they get this thing resolved," Weaver said.

"Few people doubt they have good assets -- hospitals and market share. The question is how long does the investigation keep Columbia from being able to get that value unleashed to shareholders," she added.
"Continued press sensationalism of the Columbia situation is hitting the tape (share price) on a daily basis," said Joel Ray, a Wheat First Butcher Singer analyst.
"It's playing out in the press more than in the courts, continuing to wear and tear and burden the stock," he added.

Ray said he saw no indications of extensive fraud. But he added the federal government could prevent Columbia from participation in the Medicare program if that scenario was proven -- jeopardizing 40 percent of the company's $20 billion in annual revenues.
Columbia spokesman Jeff Prescott declined to comment whether the company was concerned about that worst-case- scenario, calling it "a speculative area."
And he said he was unable to comment about alleged destruction of documents.
"Any positions we're going to take on pending legal issues, we'll do in court," he added.
(( Ransdell Pierson, New York Newsdesk, 212 859-1736))
